Amin al-Husseini.fact: He accepted the pardon only in the wake of the death of his half-brother, the mufti Kamil al-Husayni, in March 1921. A year earlier the British had replaced Musa al-Husayni as Mayor of Jerusalem with Raghib al-Nashashibi.

Vikramaditya I.question: The _____ was Chalukya Emperor from 655 to 680.
Vikramaditya I.fact: Vikramaditya I (reigned 655–680) was the third son and followed his father, Pulakeshi II on to the Chalukya throne.

Al-Masudi.fact: It is believed that he was a member of Banu Hudhayl tribe of Arabs.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: His journeys took him to most of the _____ provinces, Armenia, Georgia and other region of the Caspian Sea; as well as to Arabia, Syria and Egypt
Al-Masudi.fact: His journeys took him to most of the Persian provinces, Armenia, Georgia and other region of the Caspian Sea; as well as to Arabia, Syria and Egypt. Al-Masʿudi may have reached Sri Lanka and China although he is known to have met Abu Zayd al-Sirafi on the coast of the Persian Gulf and received information on China from him.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: He also travelled to the _____, and other parts of India, especially the western coast; and he voyaged more than once to East Africa
Al-Masudi.fact: He also travelled to the Indus Valley, and other parts of India, especially the western coast; and he voyaged more than once to East Africa.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: He also sailed on the _____, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean and the Caspian
Al-Masudi.fact: He also sailed on the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean and the Caspian.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Al-Masʿudi may have reached _____ and China although he is known to have met Abu Zayd al-Sirafi on the coast of the Persian Gulf and received information on China from him
Al-Masudi.fact: Al-Masʿudi may have reached Sri Lanka and China although he is known to have met Abu Zayd al-Sirafi on the coast of the Persian Gulf and received information on China from him.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: He presumably gathered information on _____ from the Byzantine admiral, Leo of Tripoli, a convert-to-Islam whom he met in Syria where his last years were divided between there and Egypt
Al-Masudi.fact: He presumably gathered information on Byzantium from the Byzantine admiral, Leo of Tripoli, a convert-to-Islam whom he met in Syria where his last years were divided between there and Egypt.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: In Egypt he found a copy of a _____ king list from Clovis to Louis IV that had been written by an Andalusian bishop
Al-Masudi.fact: In Egypt he found a copy of a Frankish king list from Clovis to Louis IV that had been written by an Andalusian bishop.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Little is known of his means and funding of his extensive travels within and beyond the lands of _____, and it has been speculated that like many travelers he was involved in trade
Al-Masudi.fact: He presumably gathered information on Byzantium from the Byzantine admiral, Leo of Tripoli, a convert-to-Islam whom he met in Syria where his last years were divided between there and Egypt. Little is known of his means and funding of his extensive travels within and beyond the lands of Islam, and it has been speculated that like many travelers he was involved in trade.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: We know that al-Masʿudi wrote a revised edition of Murūj al-_____ in 956 CE; however, only a draft version from 947 is extant
Al-Masudi.fact: We know that al-Masʿudi wrote a revised edition of Murūj al-Dhahab in 956 CE; however, only a draft version from 947 is extant. Al-Masʿudi in his Tanbīh states that the revised edition of Murūj al-Dhahab contained 365 chapters.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Al-Masʿudi in his Tanbīh states that the revised edition of Murūj al-_____ contained 365 chapters
Al-Masudi.fact: We know that al-Masʿudi wrote a revised edition of Murūj al-Dhahab in 956 CE; however, only a draft version from 947 is extant. Al-Masʿudi in his Tanbīh states that the revised edition of Murūj al-Dhahab contained 365 chapters.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Major cities like _____ had large public libraries and many individuals, such as as-Suli, a friend of al-Mas‘udi's, had private libraries, often containing thousands of volumes
Al-Masudi.fact: Major cities like Baghdad had large public libraries and many individuals, such as as-Suli, a friend of al-Mas‘udi's, had private libraries, often containing thousands of volumes.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: Early in the Abbasid era the art of papermaking was brought to the Islamic world by Chinese prisoners after the battle of Talas and most large towns and cities had paper mills.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: Al-Mas'udi was a pupil, or junior colleague, of prominent intellectuals, including the philologists al-Zajjaj, Ibn Duraid, Niftawayh and ibn Anbari.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: He was acquainted with famous poets, including _____, whom he probably met in Aleppo
Al-Masudi.fact: He was acquainted with famous poets, including Kashajim, whom he probably met in Aleppo.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: He was well read in philosophy, the works of al-Kindi and al-Razi, the _____ thought of al-Farabi and the Platonic writings
Al-Masudi.fact: He was well read in philosophy, the works of al-Kindi and al-Razi, the Aristotelian thought of al-Farabi and the Platonic writings.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: It is probable that al-Masʿudi met al-Razi and al-_____, but only a meeting with al-Farabi's pupil Yahya ibn Adi, of whom he spoke highly, is recorded
Al-Masudi.fact: He was well read in philosophy, the works of al-Kindi and al-Razi, the Aristotelian thought of al-Farabi and the Platonic writings. It is probable that al-Masʿudi met al-Razi and al-Farabi, but only a meeting with al-Farabi's pupil Yahya ibn Adi, of whom he spoke highly, is recorded.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: He was familiar with the medical work of Galen, with _____ astronomy, with the geographical work of Marinus and with the studies of Islamic geographers and astronomers
Al-Masudi.fact: He was familiar with the medical work of Galen, with Ptolemaic astronomy, with the geographical work of Marinus and with the studies of Islamic geographers and astronomers.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Then the _____ religion appeared in Byzantium and the centres of learning were eliminated, their vestiges effaced and the edifice of Greek learning was obliterated
Al-Masudi.fact: Then the Christian religion appeared in Byzantium and the centres of learning were eliminated, their vestiges effaced and the edifice of Greek learning was obliterated.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Everything the ancient _____ had brought to light vanished, and the discoveries of the ancients were altered beyond recognition
Al-Masudi.fact: Everything the ancient Greeks had brought to light vanished, and the discoveries of the ancients were altered beyond recognition.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: According to al-Subki, al-Mas'udi was a student of _____, the leading scholar of the Shafi'ite school
Al-Masudi.fact: According to al-Subki, al-Mas'udi was a student of Ibn Surayj, the leading scholar of the Shafi'ite school. Al-Subki claimed he found al-Mas'udi's notes of Ibn Surayj's lectures.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Al-Subki claimed he found al-Mas'udi's notes of _____'s lectures
Al-Masudi.fact: According to al-Subki, al-Mas'udi was a student of Ibn Surayj, the leading scholar of the Shafi'ite school. Al-Subki claimed he found al-Mas'udi's notes of Ibn Surayj's lectures.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Al-Mas'udi also met _____'ites during his stay in Egypt
Al-Masudi.fact: According to al-Subki, al-Mas'udi was a student of Ibn Surayj, the leading scholar of the Shafi'ite school. Al-Mas'udi also met Shafi'ites during his stay in Egypt.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: He met _____ in Baghdad and Aleppo such as Ibn Jabir and Niftawayh; modern scholarship leans toward the view that al-Mas'udi was an adherent of the latter school
Al-Masudi.fact: He met Zahirites in Baghdad and Aleppo such as Ibn Jabir and Niftawayh; modern scholarship leans toward the view that al-Mas'udi was an adherent of the latter school.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Al-Masʿudi knew leading Mu'tazilites, including al-Jubba, al-Nawbakhti, _____ al-Jurjani and Abu'l-Qasim al-Balkhi al-Ka'bi
Al-Masudi.fact: Al-Masʿudi knew leading Mu'tazilites, including al-Jubba, al-Nawbakhti, Ibn Abdak al-Jurjani and Abu'l-Qasim al-Balkhi al-Ka'bi.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: However, Shboul points out that his extant works do not specifically state that he was.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Al-Mas'udi included the history of the ancient civilizations that had occupied the land upon which _____ later spread
Al-Masudi.fact: Al-Mas'udi included the history of the ancient civilizations that had occupied the land upon which Islam later spread.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: He mentions the _____, Babylonians, Egyptians and Persians among others
Al-Masudi.fact: He mentions the Assyrians, Babylonians, Egyptians and Persians among others. He is also the only Arab historian to refer (albeit indirectly) to the kingdom of Urartu, when he speaks about the wars between the Assyrians (led by the legendary Queen Semiramis) and Armenians (led by King Ara the Handsome).

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Al-Masʿudi was aware of the influence of ancient _____ on Persia
Al-Masudi.fact: He mentions the Assyrians, Babylonians, Egyptians and Persians among others. Al-Masʿudi was aware of the influence of ancient Babylon on Persia.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: He had access to a wealth of translations by scholars such as Abdullah ibn al-Muqaffa from _____ into Arabic
Al-Masudi.fact: He had access to a wealth of translations by scholars such as Abdullah ibn al-Muqaffa from Middle Persian into Arabic.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: In his travels, he also personally consulted _____ scholars and Zoroastrian priests
Al-Masudi.fact: He had access to a wealth of translations by scholars such as Abdullah ibn al-Muqaffa from Middle Persian into Arabic. In his travels, he also personally consulted Persian scholars and Zoroastrian priests.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: Like other _____ historians, he was unclear on the Achaemenid dynasty, though he knew of Kurush (Cyrus the Great)
Al-Masudi.fact: He had access to a wealth of translations by scholars such as Abdullah ibn al-Muqaffa from Middle Persian into Arabic. Like other Arabic historians, he was unclear on the Achaemenid dynasty, though he knew of Kurush (Cyrus the Great).

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: He was much clearer on the more recent dynasties and his estimation of the time between _____ the Great and Ardashir is much more accurately depicted than it is in al-Tabari
Al-Masudi.fact: He was much clearer on the more recent dynasties and his estimation of the time between Alexander the Great and Ardashir is much more accurately depicted than it is in al-Tabari. Again, like other Arabic historians, he was unclear on Greece before the Macedonian dynasty that produced Alexander the Great.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: His wide-ranging interests included the _____ and the Romans
Al-Masudi.fact: His wide-ranging interests included the Greeks and the Romans.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: Like other Arabic historians, he was unclear on the Achaemenid dynasty, though he knew of Kurush (Cyrus the Great). Again, like other Arabic historians, he was unclear on Greece before the Macedonian dynasty that produced Alexander the Great.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: He also seems unfamiliar with such additional aspects of Greek political life as Athenian democratic institutions.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: The same holds for Rome prior to _____
Al-Masudi.fact: The same holds for Rome prior to Caesar.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: However, he is the earliest extant Arabic author to mention the Roman founding myth of Romulus and Remus.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: In al-Masʿudi's view the greatest contribution of the _____ was philosophy
Al-Masudi.fact: In al-Masʿudi's view the greatest contribution of the Greeks was philosophy.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: He was aware of the progression of Greek philosophy from the pre-Socratics onward.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: He also was keenly interested in the earlier events of the Arabian peninsula.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages
Al-Masudi.question: He recognized that _____ had a long and rich history
Al-Masudi.fact: He also was keenly interested in the earlier events of the Arabian peninsula. He recognized that Arabia had a long and rich history.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: Other authors, even Christians writing in Arabic in the Caliphate, had less to say about the Byzantine Empire than al-Mas'udi.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: He also described the geography of many lands beyond the Abbasid Caliphate, as well as the customs and religious beliefs of many peoples.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: His brief portrayal of Southeast Asia stands out for its degree of accuracy and clarity.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: He surveyed the vast areas inhabited by Turkic peoples, commenting on what had been the extensive authority of the Khaqan, though this was no longer the case by al-Mas'udi's time. Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Al-Masudi.fact: He surveyed the vast areas inhabited by Turkic peoples, commenting on what had been the extensive authority of the Khaqan, though this was no longer the case by al-Mas'udi's time. Al-Masudi.fact: He spoke of the significance of the Khazars and provided much fresh material on them.

Al-Masudi.subject: Indian Languages

Copto-Arabic literature.fact: The early 20th century saw a surge in production, but there are no Coptic poets in Arabic comparable to the best Egyptian Muslim poets. Copto-Arabic literature.fact: Second, while Coptic was still a living language, some texts were written in Arabic but in Coptic script (a practice called allography). Finally, after having been completely supplanted as the spoken language by Arabic, Coptic was rendered as needed in Arabic script.

Euro sign.subject: Indian Languages

Euro sign.fact: The euro sign (€) is the currency sign used for the euro, the official currency of the eurozone.

Euro sign.subject: Indian Languages

Cursive.subject: Indian Languages
Cursive.question: The _____ was Style of penmanship.
Cursive.fact: Cursive (also called joined-up writing) is any style of penmanship in which characters are written joined in a flowing manner, generally for the purpose of making writing faster, in contrast to block letters. Formal cursive is generally joined, but casual cursive is a combination of joins and pen lifts.

Cursive.subject: Indian Languages

Cursive.fact: In the Arabic, Syriac, Latin, and Cyrillic scripts, many or all letters in a word are connected (while others must not), sometimes making a word one single complex stroke.

Cursive.subject: Indian Languages

Cursive.fact: Italic penmanship became popular in the 15th-century Italian Renaissance.

Cursive.fact: The individuality of the provenance of a document (see Signature) was a factor also, as opposed to machine font.

Cursive.fact: The post-World War II proliferation of the inexpensive ballpoint pen added convenience to writing by hand and eliminated the flourishes liquid ink and flexible metal tips had allowed.

Cursive.subject: Indian Languages
Cursive.question: In the _____ SAT, an American university matriculation exam, only 15 percent of the students wrote their essay answers in cursive
Cursive.fact: In the 2006 SAT, an American university matriculation exam, only 15 percent of the students wrote their essay answers in cursive.

Cursive.subject: Indian Languages
Cursive.question: Nevertheless, in _____, a survey of 200 teachers of first through third grades in all 50 American states, 90 percent of respondents said their schools required the teaching of cursive
Cursive.fact: Nevertheless, in 2007, a survey of 200 teachers of first through third grades in all 50 American states, 90 percent of respondents said their schools required the teaching of cursive.

Cursive.question: In spite of this mandate, a nationwide survey in _____ found elementary school teachers lacking formal training in teaching handwriting; only 12 percent reported having taken a course in how to teach
Cursive.fact: In spite of this mandate, a nationwide survey in 2008 found elementary school teachers lacking formal training in teaching handwriting; only 12 percent reported having taken a course in how to teach it.

Cursive.subject: Indian Languages
Cursive.question: Nationwide Common Core State Standards (which do not include instruction in cursive) were proposed in _____ and had been adopted by 44 states as of July 2011—all of which have debated whether to augme
Cursive.fact: Nationwide Common Core State Standards (which do not include instruction in cursive) were proposed in 2009 and had been adopted by 44 states as of July 2011—all of which have debated whether to augment them with cursive.

Cursive.fact: California passed cursive handwriting legislation in 2023, adding to a wave of state legislation between 2013 and 2023 that requires the incorporation of cursive handwriting into elementary education.

Cursive.subject: Indian Languages

Cursive.question: Some features of this handwriting were later adopted into _____ minuscule, the dominant form of handwriting in the medieval and early modern era
Cursive.fact: Some features of this handwriting were later adopted into Greek minuscule, the dominant form of handwriting in the medieval and early modern era. Cursive.subject: Indian Languages
Cursive.question: It was used alongside _____ until the 20th century as a shorthand script for quick writing in business and administration
Cursive.fact: It was used alongside Devanagari until the 20th century as a shorthand script for quick writing in business and administration. Due to the promotion of the Balbodh variant of Devanagari as the standard writing system for Marathi, Modi largely fell out of use by the mid-20th century.

Cursive.subject: Indian Languages
Cursive.question: Due to the promotion of the _____ variant of Devanagari as the standard writing system for Marathi, Modi largely fell out of use by the mid-20th century
Cursive.fact: Due to the promotion of the Balbodh variant of Devanagari as the standard writing system for Marathi, Modi largely fell out of use by the mid-20th century.

Cursive.subject: Indian Languages

Cursive.fact: Some characters are "broken" versions of their Devanagari counterparts.

Cursive.subject: Indian Languages
Cursive.question: While several letters resemble _____ counterparts, many of them represent different sounds
Cursive.fact: Old Roman cursive, also called majuscule cursive and capitalis cursive, was the everyday form of handwriting used for writing letters, by merchants writing business accounts, by schoolchildren learning the Latin alphabet, and even by emperors issuing commands. While several letters resemble Latin counterparts, many of them represent different sounds.

Cursive.subject: Indian Languages
Cursive.question: Most children in _____ schools are taught in the first grade how to write using this Russian script
Cursive.fact: Most handwritten Russian, especially personal letters and schoolwork, uses the cursive Russian (Cyrillic) alphabet although use of block letters in private writing has been rising. Most children in Russian schools are taught in the first grade how to write using this Russian script.

G.subject: Indian Languages

G.fact: G (minuscule: g) is the seventh letter of the Latin alphabet, used in the modern English alphabet, the alphabets of other Western European languages, and others worldwide. Its name in English is gee (pronounced ), plural gees.

G.fact: The lowercase version can be written in two forms: the single-storey (sometimes "opentail") g and the double-storey (sometimes "looptail") g. The latter form is used by most serif typefaces, such as Times.

G.fact: In the International Phonetic Alphabet, opentail ⟨⟩ has always represented a voiced velar plosive, while looptail ⟨⟩ represented a voiced velar fricative from 1895 to 1900.

G.subject: Indian Languages
G.question: In _____, the Council of the International Phonetic Association recognized ⟨ɡ⟩ and ⟨⟩ as typographic equivalents, and this decision was reaffirmed in 1993
G.fact: In 1948, the Council of the International Phonetic Association recognized ⟨ɡ⟩ and ⟨⟩ as typographic equivalents, and this decision was reaffirmed in 1993.

G.subject: Indian Languages

G.fact: The 1999 Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, the successor to the Principles, abandoned the recommendation and acknowledged both shapes as acceptable variants.

G.subject: Indian Languages

G.fact: On the other hand, some dialects (like Amelands) may have a phonemic /ɡ/.

Garshunography.subject: Indian Languages
Garshunography.question: The _____ was Using the script of one language to write another.
Garshunography.fact: Garshunography is the use of "the script of one language to write utterances of another language which already has a script associated with it sociolinguistically". The term "garshunography" comes from Garshuni, a term of uncertain origin that refers to the writing of the Arabic language in the Syriac script.

Garshunography.subject: Indian Languages
Garshunography.question: Likewise, for _____, writing can transition from garshunographic to nongarshunographic over time if the adopted script becomes dominant
Garshunography.fact: Likewise, for Kiraz, writing can transition from garshunographic to nongarshunographic over time if the adopted script becomes dominant.

Garshunography.subject: Indian Languages

Garshunography.fact: Both transitions are apparent in the history of Anatolian Turkish, which first adopted a variety of Arabic script and then transitioned to a variety of Latin script.

Garshunography.subject: Indian Languages
Garshunography.question: The Armenian, _____, Kurdish, Malayalam, Persian, Sogdian and Turkish languages have all been written at some point in Syriac script
Garshunography.fact: The Armenian, Azerbaijani, Kurdish, Malayalam, Persian, Sogdian and Turkish languages have all been written at some point in Syriac script.

Garshunography.subject: Indian Languages
Garshunography.question: Since at least the 13th century, _____ have written Arabic texts in Samaritan script in order to mark them as sacred
Garshunography.fact: Since at least the 13th century, Samaritans have written Arabic texts in Samaritan script in order to mark them as sacred.

Garshunography.subject: Indian Languages
Garshunography.question: Besides aljamiado, there are other examples of Arabic script used for languages with scripts of their own, including _____, Serbo-Croatian Arebica and Chinese Xiao'erjing
Garshunography.fact: Besides aljamiado, there are other examples of Arabic script used for languages with scripts of their own, including Belarusian Arabitsa, Serbo-Croatian Arebica and Chinese Xiao'erjing.

Garshunography.subject: Indian Languages
Garshunography.question: William Worrell argues that the _____ went through three stages in its contact with Arabic
Garshunography.fact: William Worrell argues that the Coptic Egyptian went through three stages in its contact with Arabic.

Garshunography.subject: Indian Languages
Garshunography.question: Second, while still a living language, some texts were written in _____ but in the Coptic alphabet

Garshunography.subject: Indian Languages
Garshunography.question: Finally, after having been completely supplanted as the spoken and written language by _____, Coptic was rendered as needed in Arabic script
Garshunography.fact: William Worrell argues that the Coptic Egyptian went through three stages in its contact with Arabic. First, it borrowed the odd Arabic word.

Garshunography.subject: Indian Languages
Garshunography.question: There are surviving examples of blockprinted amulets containing Arabic words in the Coptic alphabet, probably intended to be sold to _____
Garshunography.fact: There are surviving examples of blockprinted amulets containing Arabic words in the Coptic alphabet, probably intended to be sold to Coptic Christians.

Garshunography.subject: Indian Languages

Garshunography.fact: In the case of the Arabic–Old French glossary from the period of the Crusades, French was written in the Coptic alphabet.

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: The _____ was Effort to map CJK characters in Unicode.
Han unification.fact: Han unification is an effort by the authors of Unicode and the Universal Character Set to map multiple character sets of the Han characters of the so-called CJK languages into a single set of unified characters. In the formulation of Unicode, an attempt was made to unify these variants by considering them as allographs – different glyphs representing the same "grapheme" or orthographic unit – hence, "Han unification", with the resulting character repertoire sometimes contracted to Unihan.

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: Han characters are a feature shared in common by written _____ (hanzi), Japanese (kanji), Korean (hanja) and Vietnamese (chữ Hán)
Han unification.fact: Han characters are a feature shared in common by written Chinese (hanzi), Japanese (kanji), Korean (hanja) and Vietnamese (chữ Hán). Modern Chinese, Japanese and Korean typefaces typically use regional or historical variants of a given Han character.

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: Modern Chinese, _____ and Korean typefaces typically use regional or historical variants of a given Han character
Han unification.fact: Han characters are a feature shared in common by written Chinese (hanzi), Japanese (kanji), Korean (hanja) and Vietnamese (chữ Hán). Modern Chinese, Japanese and Korean typefaces typically use regional or historical variants of a given Han character.

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: Nevertheless, many characters have regional variants assigned to different code points, such as _____ 個 (U+500B) versus Simplified 个 (U+4E2A)
Han unification.fact: Nevertheless, many characters have regional variants assigned to different code points, such as Traditional 個 (U+500B) versus Simplified 个 (U+4E2A).

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: The Ideographic Research Group (IRG), made up of experts from the _____-speaking countries, North and South Korea, Japan, Vietnam, and other countries, is responsible for the process
Han unification.fact: Modern Chinese, Japanese and Korean typefaces typically use regional or historical variants of a given Han character. The Ideographic Research Group (IRG), made up of experts from the Chinese-speaking countries, North and South Korea, Japan, Vietnam, and other countries, is responsible for the process.

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: One rationale was the desire to limit the size of the full _____ character set, where CJK characters as represented by discrete ideograms may approach or exceed 100,000 characters
Han unification.fact: In the formulation of Unicode, an attempt was made to unify these variants by considering them as allographs – different glyphs representing the same "grapheme" or orthographic unit – hence, "Han unification", with the resulting character repertoire sometimes contracted to Unihan. One rationale was the desire to limit the size of the full Unicode character set, where CJK characters as represented by discrete ideograms may approach or exceed 100,000 characters.

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: Version 1 of _____ was designed to fit into 16 bits and only 20,940 characters (32%) out of the possible 65,536 were reserved for these CJK Unified Ideographs
Han unification.fact: One rationale was the desire to limit the size of the full Unicode character set, where CJK characters as represented by discrete ideograms may approach or exceed 100,000 characters. Version 1 of Unicode was designed to fit into 16 bits and only 20,940 characters (32%) out of the possible 65,536 were reserved for these CJK Unified Ideographs.

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: There are four basic traditions for _____ character shapes: traditional Chinese, simplified Chinese, Japanese, and Korean
Han unification.fact: There are four basic traditions for East Asian character shapes: traditional Chinese, simplified Chinese, Japanese, and Korean.

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: For example, the traditional _____ glyph for "grass" uses four strokes for the "grass" radical [⺿], whereas the simplified Chinese, Japanese, and Korean glyphs [⺾] use three
Han unification.fact: There are four basic traditions for East Asian character shapes: traditional Chinese, simplified Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. For example, the traditional Chinese glyph for "grass" uses four strokes for the "grass" radical [⺿], whereas the simplified Chinese, Japanese, and Korean glyphs [⺾] use three.

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: But there is only one _____ point for the grass character (U+8349) [草] regardless of writing system
Han unification.fact: But there is only one Unicode point for the grass character (U+8349) [草] regardless of writing system. In fact, the three ideographs for "one" (一, 壹, or 壱) are encoded separately in Unicode, as they are not considered national variants.

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: In fact, the three ideographs for "one" (一, 壹, or 壱) are encoded separately in _____, as they are not considered national variants
Han unification.fact: But there is only one Unicode point for the grass character (U+8349) [草] regardless of writing system. In fact, the three ideographs for "one" (一, 壹, or 壱) are encoded separately in Unicode, as they are not considered national variants.

Han unification.subject: Indian Languages
Han unification.question: Another example is the ideograph for "one," which is different in _____, Japanese, and Korean
Han unification.fact: For example, the traditional Chinese glyph for "grass" uses four strokes for the "grass" radical [⺿], whereas the simplified Chinese, Japanese, and Korean glyphs [⺾] use three. Another example is the ideograph for "one," which is different in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean.

Han unification.question: (See Kanji § _____ reform and lists of kanji
Han unification.fact: (See Kanji § Orthographic reform and lists of kanji.
